title: How to Validate Your AI Startup Idea FAST (Step-by-Step)
normalization: Concatenate utf8 segments per caption event; retain event start and duration; whitespace trim only.

segments.text: 90% of startups fail. And the number one
reason isn't running out of money. It's
building something no one wants. And I
know this because I've lived it multiple
times. And it's [music] painful. But
when I launched my latest startup, RB2B,
we went from idea to 1 million in just 6
weeks. The difference wasn't luck. It
was how I validated the idea before
writing a single line of code. From that
experience, combined with building and
selling my SAS company, Robbley, for
eight figures, and then bootstrapping
Retention.com, to over 20 million ARR,
I've learned that validation is
everything. So, in this video, I'm going
to break down the exact step-by-step
process I use to validate RB2B before
building it, and how you can copy the
same system to validate any AI startup
idea and figure out if people actually
want it before you build it. Let's get
into it. Here's why most AI startup
founders get validation wrong. As I've
said, I've been through this. Let me
take you back to 2012 when I started my
first startup, Robblely Email Marketing.
I was 32 years old. I'd been on Wall
Street for 10 years. I had zero relevant
startup experience. My plan was to build
an email marketing platform, basically a
near replica of Mailchimp. It took us 18
months to build because I thought we
needed 85% of their features before we
could launch. This entire time I spoke
to zero potential customers. I sat
around and waited for the product to be
done. When it was finally ready in
January of 2014, I modeled out 800
paying customers for month one and we
ended up getting 10. It was totally
embarrassing. By some act of God, we
found a growth hack that got us to 3
million ARR. We figured out how to crawl
the internet for signup widgets from
competitors like Constant Contact and
Mailchimp and made their customers a 50%
more opens for half the price offer. But
that was a stroke of luck and the only
reason that the business survived. But
then we got completely stuck. We topped
out at 3 million ARR and shrunk at about
a half a percent per month over the next
several years. I tried to break out of
it. I spent over a million dollars
building an entirely new email marketing
application to go after the market
segment above Mailchimp. Again, we
didn't talk to anyone while we were
building it. When we launched at a trade
show, people's eyes glazed over. And it
turns out around 10 other vendors were
already filling that hole that we
thought we were filling. We literally
deleted the code and moved on. a million
dollars in a full year of my life
completely wasted. That experience
taught me the most important lesson in
startups and AI. Your intuition is a
horrible indicator of what the market
actually wants. I didn't speak to anyone
before we launched. I growth hack way
too early and I tried to scale something
that wasn't good enough to scale. So,
let me show you the framework I use now.
The one that took RB2B from zero to 1
million ARR in 6 weeks. Step one is you
start with conversations, not code. The
biggest mistake I see founders make, and
I made it myself, is building before you
talk to anyone. Building in stealth mode
is one of the dumbest things a startup
founder can do. Nobody's going to steal
your idea. Anybody who is capable of
executing your idea is already busy
doing something else. You need feedback
from the market more than you need your
precious secrecy. Before you write a
single line of code, you need a sizzling
oneliner. This is an exciting,
provocative statement that clearly
describes the problem you're solving. It
should be a clear, concise and very
differentiated statement. Anything else
will fall on deaf ears. For RB2B, our
sizzling oneliner was person level
website visitor identification. Six
words and immediately people understood
the value of what we were talking about.
We use this oneliner to open more than
300 discovery conversations and it
remains the headline on our website to
this day. Now, you need to get as many
client calls as humanly possible with
RB2B. My co-founder, Santos, and I did
over 300 discovery calls between October
2023 and March 2024. These weren't sales
calls. They were validation calls. We
were trying to understand exactly what
people wanted and how much they'd be
willing to pay for it. Here's how we got
those calls. I'd been building an
audience on LinkedIn by sharing the real
messy process of running retention.com,
my other business, including all the
failures. I pivoted my LinkedIn content
entirely towards B2B SAS and had three
of the most banger posts in a row I've
ever had that got 1.8 million
impressions combined, three posts in a
row. I started writing posting the
shortcomings of company level
identification. And at the end of every
post, I put a simple CTA. DM me if you
want to identify your website visitors
and push their LinkedIn profiles to
Slack. It's 100% free. My DMs absolutely
exploded. Hundreds of messages. But even
if you don't have an audience yet, you
can still get these calls. Start with
your personal network on LinkedIn. See
if anyone connected to you is in your
ideal customer profile and send them a
direct message. If they're connected to
someone you know, ask for an intro.
Offer paid advisory roles to directors
and below. Fun fact, my co-founder Diana
Ross, I landed her using this exact
LinkedIn DM template. And here's the
approach that I love from Alina
Vanderberg. She was pre-revenue at
what's now a 40 million ARR startup
called Chili Piper. She went to every
single B2B meetup in New York, observed
who the most connected people were in
the room and approached them with a
notepad and a drawing of original
product vision on it. She asked them,
"Would you buy something like this? And
if not, what would have to change?" She
still does this 9 years later. Once
you're on these calls, here are the
exact questions to ask. Number one, do
you understand the problem I'm trying to
solve? If they don't get it, your
messaging is off. Number two, do you
have this problem? If they don't,
they're not your ideal customer. Number
three, how are you solving this problem
today? This tells you who your real
competition is. Number four, would you
pay for the solution if I could get it
to you tomorrow? And watch their body
language, not just their words. People
love lying to people who are starting
startups. They just want to be friendly.
Number five, what else would the
solution have to do for you to pay for
it? This is gold. And this is where they
tell you what your road map should look
like. And number six, I'm thinking of
charging X per month. Would you pay
that? Always test pricing conversation.
Your gut is a terrible indicator. The
more calls you do, the better your pitch
will get and a pattern will soon emerge.
With RB2B, the pattern was crystal
clear. Everyone was frustrated with
company level identification because it
told them things like someone from
Microsoft in Atlanta is on your site,
which is completely useless. They wanted
to know the actual person, the pages
they looked at, and how to follow up
immediately. Once we saw same pattern
across hundreds of calls, we knew we had
something. Step two is try to get people
to pay before you build. Positive
feedback is not validation. Yeah, that
sounds interesting means absolutely
nothing. Very few people will be honest
with you about your idea. People have a
bias to be nice. If for no other reason
than to end the conversation sooner. The
single best way to figure out if someone
actually likes your idea is to get them
to hand you money. Even $1 is incredibly
powerful. So much more powerful than
words. With RB2B, we tried to get people
to pay us before the product existed. We
tried to charge $495 a month for a
spreadsheet of LinkedIn URLs. And that's
it, a spreadsheet. We didn't even have a
product and hardly anyone paid. But then
we discovered a magic moment. When we
showed people a Slack notification on
our phone with head shot [music] and
LinkedIn profile URLs popping up in real
time, and I'd say, "These people just
hit the retention.com website." Their
eyes lit up every single time. People
were saying things like, "This is nuts.
I can't believe this. This feels like
I'm cheating or something." And that gap
between [music] what people said they'd
pay us for versus what made them
genuinely react was the key insight. The
spreadsheet didn't excite anyone. But
the real-time Slack notifications, that
was a product. You need to look for
magic moments in every single
interaction you have with your
customers. Overjoyed facial expressions,
emails that say they can't believe how
good this is. Magic moments are when
unicorns are born. And here's the
question you should be asking yourself.
If I took my product away from these
users right now, how upset would they
get? the more upset they get, the more
fun you're going to have scaling. The
less upset they get, the more of a grind
your whole life is going to be. Step
three is build the absolute minimum
viable product. Once you found the thing
that makes people's eyes light up, now
you build and you build the absolute
minimum. Be ruthless about keeping your
product as lean as possible. Don't sink
time and money into developing
unnecessary features. Instead, find a
way to do what you need to do manually,
even if it's inefficient, clunky, and
feels like a time suck. You'll save
yourself a ton of cash when you realize
it's not actually what your prospects
want and therefore you shouldn't build
it. With RB2B, we manually onboarded
beta testers by hand starting in October
2023. We sent them a pixel over email,
sent them a daily spreadsheet, also via
email, and we did this for five full
months before even putting up a website.
We could have built the tools and
automated all of that, but we didn't.
Doing this manually allowed us to talk
to customers more often, be closer to
them as they onboarded and used our
product. It let us learn things we never
would have learned with automation, and
it got our product into customers hands
months earlier than we would have done
otherwise. Focus on the smallest
possible niche. When Nathan Barry
launched ConvertKit, which is now over
50 million ARR, bootstrapped, he didn't
launch an email marketing tool for
everybody. He started by saying it was
an email marketing tool for food
bloggers. And after getting the first
few influential food bloggers, it was
easy to reach out to other food bloggers
because the most famous ones had already
switched from Mailchimp. Over the years,
he expanded into many other niches, but
he started with a super tight niche.
Remember, the riches are in the niches,
and no niche is too small if you
absolutely dominate it. So, don't rush
to automate. Stay manual as long as you
possibly can. The insights you get in
that phase are worth more than any
feature you could build. Nothing is more
highly correlated to your success than
how well you navigate the discovery and
product market fit process. Step four is
test pricing with real users. I'm going
to be brutally honest with you. This is
where we really struggled. When we
officially launched RB2B, here's how we
structured the offer. I'd always admired
Mailchimp's premium model, so we decided
to give the LinkedIn push to Slack
completely free forever. Competitors
were charging hundreds of thousands of
dollars, and all they did was tell you
the company name. They didn't even ID
the actual person. Our paid tier was
$149 a month for business emails, plus
all integrations and access to Slack.
This generated over 1,600 weight list
signups and 300 meetings in just a few
months. But shortly thereafter, we hit a
brutal wall. We had 3,000 signups and
only 13 paying customers. That's a
terrible conversion rate, and it was
keeping me up at night. Most founders
would hide this. I did exactly the
opposite. I posted about the problem
constantly on LinkedIn. I was completely
transparent about the real numbers.
Commenters helped me figure out the
pricing. They gave me direct feedback on
exactly what it should look like. We
fixed the pricing based on that feedback
and got to a 12.5% touchless free-to-
paid conversion rate. Meaning that 12.5%
of free users upgrade to paid without us
doing anything. No sales calls, no
demos, just the product selling itself.
That's the unlock we needed. After
fixing this pricing, growth exploded. We
hit 1 million ARR in just 6 weeks. And
by the way, if you want to see what this
looks like in practice, you can start by
identifying your own visitors for free
by clicking the first link in the
description. It takes less than five
minutes to set up and will push LinkedIn
profiles of your website visitors to
Slack completely free. Step five is how
you know you've actually achieved
product market fit. A lot of founders
think they have product market fit when
they don't and they have some revenue,
some users, and they think it's time to
scale. They hire a bunch of people, turn
on all the paid channels, and wonder why
nothing [music] works. I've been there.
At retention.com, we figured out that
large Shopify stores were our ICP, and
we experienced the most insane product
market fit I've ever seen. We were the
only vendor who did what we did in the
entire Shopify ecosystem, and there was
more inbound demand than we had
salespeople to take demos. We were
closing $30,000 deals in 7 days with an
80% close rate, and we scaled to 12
million AR with just six people. So, I
hired 50 people in 60 days because I
thought we were ready to scale. called
my shot on LinkedIn and I predicted we'd
triple revenue from 15 million to 45
million in a year. Instead, we barely
grew 40%. We'd been overselling.
Competitors copied our product and
undercut us. And I had to let go of my
entire BDR team. That happened because I
confused early traction with true
product market fit. Here's what real
product market fit actually looks like.
And until you have it, you don't know.
Don't run ads. Don't do SEO. Don't work
with influencers. And don't seek out
UGC. Do not build a partner program. And
do not sponsor newsletters. Only do
manual things with onetoone
conversations until you get there.
Nothing will work if you don't have
product market fit. Everything will work
if you do. Here are the signals that you
actually have it. You have very strong
word of mouth and high customer
retention. If you did nothing, you would
see exponential growth in your business.
You see people enduring a horrible user
experience, but saying they love your
product. For example, at retention.com,
people were using our identity features,
downloading data, and manually uploading
into Clavio and telling us they couldn't
live without it. This was a very strong
sign of product market fit. People
willing to prepay for things in your
product that are not even there yet is
another great sign. And it feels like
the market is pulling product out of you
instead of you pushing product into the
market. And last, but not least, your
customers would be livid if you took the
product away. If you don't have these
signals, stay in validation mode. Keep
having conversations. Keep iterating.
Keep doing things manually. The key is
staying tiny until you get to the point
where people would be infuriated if you
took the product away. The validation
phase is something not to rush through.
It's the foundation. Everything else is
built on. When we had real product
market fit at RB2B, growth took care of
itself. We went from 1 million to 4
million to 7 million AR with a team of
just three people. But none of that
would have been possible if we didn't do
the validation work first. Now, if
you've already validated your AI startup
idea and you're ready to start growing,
one of the fastest ways to generate
leads is to know exactly who's visiting
